forras_nev: Institute for the Future of Education
cim_eredeti: Childhood’s Future Will Not Be Decided by Artificial Intelligence: We Will Decide It - Observatory
szoveg_eredeti:
An entire generation is growing up using something that, until recently, did not exist: children and adolescents converse, learn, create, and seek advice (and even comfort) from artificial intelligence systems that respond almost instantaneously and with a surprising appearance of security.

This is not a futuristic prediction. It is happening now.

UNICEF (2026) warns that children are adopting artificial intelligence technologies more than three times faster than adults. Based on representative surveys conducted in ten countries, including Mexico, the agency estimates that at least 20 million children and adolescents aged 12 to 17 have used AI. Approximately 13 million reported using it to support their learning and schoolwork.

However, another, more disturbing statistic is that more than two million, about one in ten, said they turn to AI for advice on matters that concern them (UNICEF, 2026).

This is where the nature of the debate changes. We are no longer just talking about a student using a chatbot to solve math problems faster. Now our discussion includes adolescents who share their fears, doubts, or personal problems with a machine before discussing such things with their parents, teachers, or friends.

UNICEF (2026) summarizes it clearly: artificial intelligence is already part of our lives and is transforming childhood worldwide, for better or worse. The problem is that its adoption is outpacing the rules, research, and protection mechanisms designed specifically for minors.

It would be a mistake to present artificial intelligence solely as a threat. Used well, it can become an extraordinary educational tool. It can explain a concept multiple times without losing patience, adapt exercises to the student’s level, translate content, provide immediate feedback, stimulate creativity, and expand access to knowledge, among many other examples

The Brookings Institution specifically recognizes this potential. Well-designed AI tools can enrich learning when they are part of a solid pedagogical strategy. The problem arises when they stop being instruments for learning and become substitutes for the learning process (Burns et al., 2026).

The difference may seem small, but it is fundamental:

Asking AI to “help me understand this problem” is different from telling it to “solve it for me.”

The PISA 2025 results raise an important red flag. More than 760,000 15-year-old students from 91 countries and economies participated in the assessment. For the first time, PISA thoroughly analyzed how students use digital tools and artificial intelligence to learn (OECD, 2026).

The results do not justify claiming that AI, on its own, causes lower academic performance. These are mainly associations, and the patterns depend on how the technology is used. However, the signal is strong enough to warrant attention: students who use AI tools more frequently for particular academic tasks tend to show less favorable educational outcomes than those who use them less or differently (OECD, 2026).

Andreas Schleicher, Director of Education and Skills at the OECD, uses a powerful analogy: just as no one improves their physical condition simply by watching sports, learning does not happen by consuming answers, but through the cognitive effort of engaging with new material.

The OECD (2026) calls this process the productive cognitive struggle: this occurs when we try to understand, connect ideas, make mistakes, correct ourselves, and finally solve a problem.

Precisely therein lies one of the greatest educational risks of AI. When technology strengthens that effort, it can scaffold learning. When it eliminates it, it becomes a crutch. Thus, a generation that systematically learns while avoiding intellectual effort could develop an enormous capacity to obtain answers and, paradoxically, a diminished capacity to construct them.

Artificial intelligence has one particularly seductive characteristic: it responds fluently. An answer can be wrong and yet sound perfectly reasonable.

Therefore, AI literacy in this era cannot mean just knowing how to use digital tools. It requires learning to concentrate, interpret, cross-reference, synthesize, argue, and question the information received (OECD, 2026).

This radically transforms the role of schools. For decades, we taught students how to find information. Now we must teach them something more difficult: how to intelligently distrust a perfectly worded answer.

The fundamental skill of the future may not be formulating the best prompt, but knowing how to stop after receiving an answer and asking: How do I know this is true?

The risk is not the same at age 4 as at 16

Another mistake would be to speak of “children” as if a four-year-old and a sixteen-year-old had the same cognitive, emotional, and social abilities.

A review published in Pediatrics by researchers affiliated with Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia underscores precisely the need to analyze artificial intelligence from a developmental perspective. The potential effects change significantly between early childhood, middle childhood, and adolescence (Grundmeier et al., 2026).

In early childhood, certain applications can foster language, creativity, or learning. However, young children are still developing their understanding of what is real, who has intentions, and what the difference is between a person and a technological representation. Human interaction remains irreplaceable.

During middle childhood, AI can stimulate curiosity, personalize explanations, and promote creativity. At the same time, risks arise from misinformation, privacy concerns, dependence on automated responses, and the substitution of effort required to complete school tasks.

In adolescence, the issue takes on an additional dimension. Artificial intelligence can become not only an academic tool, but also an emotional confidant. This occurs precisely during a stage when identity, autonomy, interpersonal relationships, and coping mechanisms for frustration and conflict are formed (Grundmeier et al., 2026).

The specialists’ warning is super relevant: AI should be understood as a tool, not as a friend or a caregiver.

This question is perhaps even more important than the discussion about school assignments.

Adolescence is a crucial stage for asking oneself who I am, what I think, whom I trust, and whom I want to become. An increasingly large part of this exploration now occurs through conversations with artificial intelligence systems.

The risk is not simply that an adolescent “talks to a computer.” The problem arises when a technology designed to generate plausible responses starts to fill roles traditionally built on human relationships: friendship, trust, guidance, conflict, reconciliation, and companionship.

Recent pediatric research warns of the risks of developing false perceptions of AI as a friend or caregiver, as well as privacy and misinformation concerns (Grundmeier et al., 2026).

Personal growth is not achieved by receiving good answers; a human being evolves by learning to interpret silences, deal with disagreements, recognize emotions, tolerate frustrations, get to know other people, and discover that the world does not have an immediate solution to our needs. No chatbot should replace this learning.

One of the most extensive international research studies on generative AI and education to date was conducted by the Brookings Institution’s Center for Universal Education.

Over more than a year, the team reviewed more than 400 research studies and conducted interviews, focus groups, and consultations with more than 500 students, teachers, families, education leaders, technologists, and specialists from 50 countries (Burns et al., 2026).

“At this point in its trajectory, the risks of utilizing generative AI in children’s education overshadow its benefits.” (Burns et al., 2026).

cim: UNICEF-felmérés: a gyerekek háromszor gyorsabban fogadják el az AI-t
lead: Az OECD és az UNICEF [kutatásai](https://observatory.tec.mx/edu-news/childhoods-future-will-not-be-decided-by-artificial-intelligence-we-will-decide-it/) szerint az **AI túlzott használata** rombolhatja a diákok kritikus gondolkodását.
osszefoglalo:
A diákok és fiatalok több mint háromszor gyorsabban kezdik el használni a mesterségesintelligencia-eszközöket, mint a felnőttek. Az UNICEF felmérése alapján több mint **20 millió 12-17 év közötti fiatal használ már AI-t**, és jelentős részük nemcsak a házi feladatokhoz, hanem **személyes problémák megbeszélésére** is a chatbotokhoz fordul.

Az OECD PISA 2025-ös adatai arra figyelmeztetnek, hogy a **gyakori AI-használat gyengébb tanulmányi eredményekkel jár együtt**, ha a technológia kiváltja a szellemi erőfeszítést. Ha a diákok a feladatok önálló megoldása helyett készen kapják a válaszokat, elmarad a tanuláshoz szükséges kognitív folyamat.

A [kutatók kiemelik](https://observatory.tec.mx/edu-news/childhoods-future-will-not-be-decided-by-artificial-intelligence-we-will-decide-it/), hogy a korai gyermekkortól a kamaszkorig terjedő időszakban az AI nem helyettesítheti a humán kapcsolatokat. A **legnagyobb kockázatot az jelenti**, ha a fiatalok bizalmasként vagy barátként tekintenek az algoritmikus rendszerekre.
miert_szamit: Az oktatási szakembereknek meg kell érteniük, hogy a fiatalabb generációk AI-használata **alapjaiban változtatja meg az információkeresési és tanulási szokásokat**, ami a [friss elemzés](https://observatory.tec.mx/edu-news/childhoods-future-will-not-be-decided-by-artificial-intelligence-we-will-decide-it/) szerint teljesen új oktatási stratégiát igényel.

prioritas.indok: Érdekes UNICEF adatok a gyermekek AI-használatáról, de inkább általános elemzés mintsem konkrét technológiai hír. Forrás-tapasztalat: -6.
prioritas.cim_hu: A gyerekek háromszor gyorsabban szoknak rá az AI-ra, mint a felnőttek
prioritas.lead_hu: Az UNICEF adatai szerint a gyerekek és fiatalok több mint háromszor gyorsabban terjedő ütemben kezdtek el mesterséges intelligenciát használni, mint a felnőttek. A szakértők a felelősségvállalás fontosságára figyelmeztetnek.

tenyellenorzes.esemeny: Az UNICEF, az OECD és a Brookings Institution kutatásai szerint a gyerekek és fiatalok az felnőtteknél lényegesen gyorsabban fogadják el az AI-t, ami a kognitív erőfeszítés kiváltása esetén ronthatja a tanulási teljesítményt és a kritikus gondolkodást.
hibak: A hír szövegéből és a mezőkből teljesen hiányoznak a kötelező beszédes hivatkozások ([szöveg](url) linkek) a forrásra.
A lead karakterszáma (139 karakter) rendben van, de a meglévő elvárás szerint minden bekezdésben (így a leadben is) kötelező félkövér **kiemelést** és forráslinket használni.
